name: Pareidolia
description: People can perceive specific meaningful patterns—most famously faces—in random, noisy, or ambiguous stimuli. The mind completes a recognisable signal that is not objectively there.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to mascot/icon/illustration design, camera/computer-vision outputs, generative-image review, and even mundane UI compositions: face-like arrangements can capture attention or trigger emotion even when accidental.
prevalence_note: Widely recognizable as a perception term, especially in visual culture and image-making, but not a core named product-UX law used constantly in design teams.

findings.description: When participants viewed pure-noise images while expecting faces or letters, they reported illusory faces about 34% of the time, and those face reports selectively recruited the right fusiform face area — direct behavioral and neural evidence for face pareidolia.
findings.source_title: Seeing Jesus in toast: Neural and behavioral correlates of face pareidolia
